pending_b.title: Designing strategic scenarios for the digital transition
pending_b.authors: Vítor Alcácer, Alexandra Tenera, Francisco Araújo, Helena Carvalho, Virgilio Cruz-Machado
pending_b.summary: Following a Design Science Research approach, the study includes a systematic literature review (20 studies) to examine existing scenario development approaches in I4.0, which did not identify any methodologies incorporating risk management. This study contributes by addressing a critical gap in risk-based scenario methodologies for I4.0 and by proposing a novel framework that integrates risk management into strategic scenario development. Abstract Strategic scenarios support decision-making under uncertainty; however, existing Industry 4.0 (I4.0) research predominantly adopts technological perspectives and does not provide methodologies that integrate risk management into scenario development.

This commentary, authored by Fellows of the Young Academy of Europe (FYAE), outlines how this governance framework is reshaping international chemical collaboration, emphasizing the urgent need for updated research security practices, the emergence of the role of Security-Safety Liaison as a practical bridge between laboratory safety, regulatory compliance, and security-sensitive research governance, and the importance of harmonized safety standards to protect European interests in an era of intensified geostrategic competition. strand_a.summary: Clarifying and optimising civil, dual-use and defence research and innovation in future EU funding programmes. CLARIFYING AND OPTIMISING CIVIL, DUAL-USE AND DEFENCE R&I IN FUTURE EU FUNDING PROGRAMMES 3 Context This input note re-emphasises and builds on the key messages of the CESAER position of 30 April 2024, ‘Strengthen dual-use technologies by enhancing EU defence funding’, which remains unchanged: FP10 should continue to be a programme with a civil focus, allowing the framework programme to continue to set the global standard for supporting excellent research & innovation and cutting-edge science & technology. Building on earlier recommendations, this note puts forward concrete proposals to clarify and optimise the integration of civil, dual-use, and defence research and innovation into future EU funding programmes by treating dual-use in two complementary ways: as a legal category for compliance purposes (‘export controlled’), and as a strategic pathway that helps identify when civil research may have potential defence relevance and how such research could, under appropriate conditions and governance, evolve along trajectories that include defence applications.

strategic_pathways.reader_title: New MSCA pilot funds longer-term postdoctoral posts to counter research precarity
strategic_pathways.reader_what: A 22.5 million euro MSCA pilot selects institutions partly on the long-term job security they offer researchers.
strategic_pathways.reader_why: Ties EU research funding to employment conditions rather than project output alone.
strategic_pathways.reader_more: Choose Europe for Science is an MSCA pilot action aimed at making European research careers more attractive by tackling precarity and turning brain drain into brain gain. Academic and non-academic organisations recruit postdoctoral researchers with a view to employment beyond the project period, and its stated novelty is that applicants are assessed partly on the longer-term professional prospects they offer. A single legal entity in a Member State or Horizon Europe associated country applies, with associated partners possible. The call budget is 22.5 million euros, capped at 3.5 million per beneficiary, and projects should recruit at least three researchers for up to five years, with MSCA covering the first two to three. Full conditions sit in the 2025 MSCA Work Programme.

dynamic_shocks.title: A security reclassification abruptly narrows access to Europe’s research infrastructures

page_guarantee.rule: New records update candidate reasoning; the shelf is re-decided each scan from recomputed maturity. No record takes a slot automatically.
page_guarantee.creative_reserve: Reserve = grounded runners-up + a creative reserve of relevant, uncontradicted hypotheses (distant, cross-domain, emerging, weak-signal or partially grounded), at least 18 and topped up toward 45, rotated across wow levels with weight on surprise. They mature into page competition when grounded.

high_order_inference.publication_policy: Stage 7 claim-native selection treats the reasoning layer as a future-hypothesis corpus. Candidate formation is broad; missing roles, thin evidence and unrun counter-evidence tests lower maturity rather than forbidding the hypothesis. Grounded candidates compete only within their wow 1-5 bucket. Each product reserves three public slots per wow level (15 total), displayed 5-4-3-2-1 three times; surplus grounded findings remain reserve and weaker hypotheses remain developing.
high_order_inference.lifecycle_policy: Claim-native stock persists as page/reserve/developing tiers. Evidence is recomputed each scan; candidates can strengthen, weaken or move between tiers as new evidence arrives. Counter-evidence and falsifier results affect maturity and can kill a contradicted hypothesis, but an unrun challenge is not a ban on future-facing reasoning.
high_order_inference.candidate_search_policy: Missing-role and falsifier queries remain ordinary scanner discovery inputs and receive no admission waiver.

scenarios_2035.method: Two uncertainties define the frame: how many resources Europe has, and how strongly Europe is connected globally. The four worlds are scenarios, not forecasts. Each has four variants built from current shocks, risks and opportunities.

axes.horizontal: Less globally connected ↔ More globally connected

scenarios.name: Connected Growth
story: Europe enters 2035 with more money, capacity and research infrastructure, while staying strongly connected to global partners. Researchers, firms and universities can work across borders easily, and Europe scales more of what it discovers.
Trace it back and you find two of today's tugs of war settled one way: “The EU has adopted a framework for science diplomacy”; “Europe is investing more in AI”.
Not everything moved. “Chips international cooperation keeps returning across the research-policy cycle.” That was true in the 2020s and it is true now.
Someone read the signs early: “Active capacity-building could expand AI-factory public procurement.” The bet worked.
The warning came early and was filed away: “Innovation-system performance is under sustained pressure.” It is now the norm.
The trade-off is exposure: deeper global links also leave Europe more dependent on decisions, suppliers and disruptions outside Europe.

bullets.label: Picture
bullets.text: Europe enters 2035 with more money, capacity and research infrastructure, while staying strongly connected to global partners. Researchers, firms and universities can work across borders easily, and Europe scales more of what it discovers.

bullets.label: A day in 2035
bullets.text: A research team in Tallinn books time on a shared European supercomputer and works with partners in Seoul and São Paulo the same week.

bullets.label: How we got here
bullets.text: Trace it back and you find two of today's tugs of war settled one way: “The EU has adopted a framework for science diplomacy”; “Europe is investing more in AI”.

bullets.label: Evidence today
bullets.text: The Council presidency frames a policy debate on strengthening Europe’s semiconductor competitiveness, resilience and strategic leadership.

scenarios.name: Independent Scale
story: By 2035, strong European investment has built more research and technology capacity, but Europe works with a narrower set of global partners. Funding and infrastructure are strong, while security, resilience and European control shape who can take part.
It grew out of two arguments the 2020s never resolved, until they were: “Research security is expanding” and “New commitments strengthen venture capital”.
Some things never changed. In the 2020s the Radar noted: “An older link between strategic investment finance and research-system governance is returning without being named.” In 2035 it still does.
One early bet paid off. The 2020s signal was “Strategic-autonomy goals could become the missing route into research-system governance.” In this world, it came true.
One risk quietly became routine: “A bottleneck in industrial competitiveness could propagate into strategic-autonomy goals.”
The trade-off is reach: Europe has more control, but fewer outside connections and less access to some global talent, markets and ideas.

frames.title: Resources × Global connectedness
frames.question: Can Europe mobilise the resources it needs, and how connected is it to the world?
frames.method: Two uncertainties define the frame: how many resources Europe has, and how strongly Europe is connected globally. The four worlds are scenarios, not forecasts. Each has four variants built from current shocks, risks and opportunities.

scenarios.name: Connected Growth
story: Europe enters 2035 with more money, capacity and research infrastructure, while staying strongly connected to global partners. Researchers, firms and universities can work across borders easily, and Europe scales more of what it discovers.
Trace it back and you find two of today's tugs of war settled one way: “The EU has adopted a framework for science diplomacy”; “Europe is investing more in AI”.
Not everything moved. “Chips international cooperation keeps returning across the research-policy cycle.” That was true in the 2020s and it is true now.
Someone read the signs early: “Active capacity-building could expand AI-factory public procurement.” The bet worked.
The warning came early and was filed away: “Innovation-system performance is under sustained pressure.” It is now the norm.
The trade-off is exposure: deeper global links also leave Europe more dependent on decisions, suppliers and disruptions outside Europe.

scenarios.name: Independent Scale
story: By 2035, strong European investment has built more research and technology capacity, but Europe works with a narrower set of global partners. Funding and infrastructure are strong, while security, resilience and European control shape who can take part.
It grew out of two arguments the 2020s never resolved, until they were: “Research security is expanding” and “New commitments strengthen venture capital”.
Some things never changed. In the 2020s the Radar noted: “An older link between strategic investment finance and research-system governance is returning without being named.” In 2035 it still does.
One early bet paid off. The 2020s signal was “Strategic-autonomy goals could become the missing route into research-system governance.” In this world, it came true.
One risk quietly became routine: “A bottleneck in industrial competitiveness could propagate into strategic-autonomy goals.”
The trade-off is reach: Europe has more control, but fewer outside connections and less access to some global talent, markets and ideas.

scenarios.name: Open Under Pressure
story: Global links remain strong in 2035, but European research and innovation operate with tight resources. Ideas and people move easily, while many European teams depend on outside capital, infrastructure or partners to scale their work.
It is the world where today's evidence toward “Horizon access capacity is expanding” and “Constraints are slowing data centres” continues.
A familiar pattern survived the decade: “An older link between research collaboration and researcher retention is returning without being named.”
One door that looked half-open in the 2020s swung wide: “New funding could expand innovation regional capacity.”
And one warning was not heeded: “Chips international cooperation is moving into practice before the rulebook catches up.” By 2035 it is simply how things work.
The trade-off is dependence: Europe stays connected, but often relies on others to finance, host or scale what it creates.

scenarios.name: Constrained Europe
story: In 2035, Europe has fewer resources and weaker global connections. Governments and institutions protect a smaller core of capabilities, while new projects, partnerships and large investments become harder to sustain.
Two pulls visible today carried it here: “Research security is expanding”, and “Constraints are slowing data infrastructure”.
Old habits held. Back then the Radar kept seeing “Defence R&I as a whole keeps returning across the research-policy cycle.” It never went away.
The lucky break was visible years ahead: “Research-system governance could become the missing route into strategic-autonomy goals.”
Nobody acted on this 2020s red flag: “Research-system governance is moving into practice before the rulebook catches up.” Now everyone lives with it.
The trade-off is ambition: Europe reduces exposure, but has less capacity to build, experiment and compete at scale.

lenses.passage: Aim of the initiative The objective of Chips Act 2 .0 is to increase the competitiveness of the European ecosystem to strengthen technological sovereignty and resilience and enhanc e crisis preparedness to ensure the EU’s security of supply and economic security. Building on the first Chips Act, the initiative aims to address these weaknesses and challenges with the objectives of: • Enhancing the EU’s capacity and security of supply in mainstream and advanced semiconductors, including AI chips; • Developing a strong user market across key industry sectors; • Increasing intelligence capabilities for crisis preparedness and response.
